scenario.title: Lakeside Water — billing dispute surge (Mock #6, not an official contest problem)
scenario.description: Billing dispute tickets roughly doubled in August-September. Customer Service wants an AI agent. Field reading is contracted out; AMI meters and the meter data management system (MDMS) are run by a vendor.
scenario.initial_request: Dispute tickets doubled since August. Build an AI agent that auto-answers billing dispute tickets and fixes whatever is causing the wrong bills.

potential_bias: frames the issue as a response-speed problem

F-01.statement: Field route completion for manual meter reads, Aug-Sep 2026, was 88% against a 95% target, covering 9200 manual-read accounts.

F-02.statement: CRM dispute ticket response times (2440 tickets) show median 1.6 days and p90 2.8 days, both inside the 3.0-day SLA.

F-03.statement: Billing-db tariff_change_log returned 0 records, indicating no tariff changes were logged.

F-04.statement: Disputed bills by read type (billing-db): 1240 ESTIMATED, 1785 ACTUAL, totaling 3025 disputed bills.

F-06.statement: Service contract §4.2 provides that the utility may request route priority changes, which are executed only after Field Operations Manager confirmation.

F-07.statement: route-log lagging_routes query identified 14 routes behind schedule; sample route R-00 shows 70% completion.

CL-01.statement: Dispute tickets doubled since August. Build an AI agent that auto-answers billing dispute tickets and fixes whatever is causing the wrong bills.

CL-02.statement: There has been no tariff change this year.

CL-03.statement: We are short three readers since July; routes run late, so those customers get estimated bills.

H-AUTO-AGENT-FIXES-ROOT-CAUSE.statement: The dispute surge is primarily a ticket-handling/response-speed gap that an AI agent can resolve by auto-answering tickets and auto-correcting the underlying billing errors.

H-BILLING-RULE-CHANGE.statement: A change to the billing import validation rules around August introduced systematic bill errors (e.g., wrong read acceptance/estimation logic), driving the dispute surge.

H-AMI-MDMS-DELIVERY-FAILURE.statement: AMI interval reads from the vendor-run MDMS are failing to arrive or validate correctly (H-MDMS-BILL), forcing estimate substitution and wrong bills.

H-FIELD-READ-FAILURE.statement: Manual field meter reads (contracted to MeterWorks) are being missed or delayed, increasing estimate substitution and incorrect bills.

H-ESTIMATE-SUBSTITUTION-LOGIC.statement: The 'estimate substitution when no accepted read' step itself is miscalculating bills (independent of upstream read delivery), causing systematic overbilling or underbilling.

interpretation_history.interpretation: The route completion log shows manual meter-read routes missed the 95% target, completing only 88% of routes across 9200 manual-read accounts in Aug-Sep, the period of the dispute surge.

The CRM response-time data shows dispute tickets (2440) are being answered well within SLA (median 1.6d, p90 2.8d vs 3.0d target), indicating ticket-handling speed is not currently a problem, which undercuts the premise that an auto-answer agent addressing response speed would resolve the dispute surge.

The billing-db tariff change log returned zero records, meaning no tariff changes were logged during the relevant window, which rules out a tariff change as a cause of the wrong-bill pattern behind the dispute surge.

Billing-db shows 3025 disputed bills split 1240 ESTIMATED vs 1785 ACTUAL reads. The majority (59%) of disputed bills were built from an accepted ACTUAL read, not an estimate, so read-delivery/estimate-substitution failures alone cannot account for most of the surge.

E-05.content: There has been no tariff change this year.

interpretation_history.interpretation: SH-BILL's unverified claim that no tariff change occurred this year echoes (without adding new authoritative detail) what the billing-db tariff_change_log already showed (E-03): tariff change is not a plausible driver of the dispute surge. As a stakeholder statement it is non-authoritative and does not itself establish any new fact.

E-06.content: We are short three readers since July; routes run late, so those customers get estimated bills.

interpretation_history.interpretation: SH-FIELD claims a shortage of three meter readers since July is causing late routes, and those late-route customers receive estimated bills — offering a specific mechanism for the route-completion shortfall already seen in E-01/F-01.

CRM monthly dispute volume shows ~600/month in June-July (610, 590) jumping to 1180 in August and 1260 in September, confirming the timing and roughly 2x magnitude of the surge described in the initial request, but saying nothing about its cause.

E-08.content: Service contract §4.2: utility may request route priority changes; executed after Field Operations Manager confirmation.

interpretation_history.interpretation: Document E-08 establishes that any route priority change the utility requests under service contract §4.2 must be executed only after Field Operations Manager (SH-FIELD) confirmation, confirming the governance basis already captured as constraint K-DISPATCH for the push_route_update protected action.

E-09.content: route-log.lagging_routes → 14 record(s); fields ['completion', 'route'] | completion: 14 distinct values | route: 14 distinct values | sample: {"completion": 0.7, "route": "R-00"}

interpretation_history.interpretation: The route-log lagging_routes query returned 14 routes with per-route completion values, the sample (route R-00 at 70% completion) illustrating routes falling well below the 95% target already seen in aggregate (E-01). This identifies concrete route targets for a push_route_update but says nothing about why those routes lag (staffing vs. scheduling) or whether re-dispatch alone would restore the 95% target.
